title: The Biggest Cost Factors in Commercial Renovation Projects
metaTitle: Commercial Renovation Cost Factors | Bridgeland Builders
metaDescription: What drives commercial renovation costs in Winnipeg: building systems, code upgrades, hidden conditions, after-hours work, and how to avoid overruns.
excerpt: The parts of a commercial renovation that move the price most, why older buildings and changes of use cost more, and the steps that keep a project from running over budget.
answer: The biggest cost drivers in a commercial renovation are usually behind the walls, not the finishes: mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire protection changes; code requirements triggered by a change of use; hidden conditions such as asbestos; after-hours or phased work; and scope changes once construction starts. Complete drawings and a contingency keep them in check.

faqs.q: What is the biggest reason commercial renovations go over budget?
faqs.a: Incomplete information at the start. When a project is priced from rough drawings, or before anyone has looked above the ceiling or checked for asbestos, the gaps show up later as change orders. Complete drawings, an investigated building, clear allowances and a contingency agreed up front prevent most of the surprises.

faqs.q: What are soft costs in a renovation?
faqs.a: Soft costs are the expenses that are not physical construction: design and engineering fees, permit fees, project management, financing costs, moving and temporary space. The City's commercial permit form counts design and project management fees in the declared construction value, which is a good reminder to include them in your budget from the start.

It can, because evening and weekend work may carry higher labour and supervision costs, and City noise rules near homes limit when loud work can happen. Compare that with the sales you would lose by closing during business hours. Bridgeland Builders offers after-hours and weekend scheduling for commercial work, and we can price both options after the on-site visit.

faqs.q: How much contingency should a commercial renovation carry?
faqs.a: There is no single right figure. Older buildings, a change of use, incomplete drawings and occupied spaces call for a larger contingency; a newer space with complete drawings needs less. BDC advises setting aside a contingency fund and buffer time because renovations often run over budget. We can help you size it once we have seen the space.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for asbestos checks before a renovation?
faqs.a: Manitoba's workplace safety regulation puts the duties on the employer and the owner: an inventory of asbestos-containing material by a person competent in identifying it, and notice to Workplace Safety and Health 5 to 10 days before work that may release it. Your lease and contract decide who pays, so ask the landlord for any existing inventory before signing.

blocks.x: Two commercial spaces of the same size can cost very different amounts to renovate. The difference is rarely the paint or flooring. It is what sits behind the walls and above the ceiling, what the building code asks for once the use changes, and how the work has to be scheduled around a business that wants to stay open.
This guide explains the main cost factors and how to control each one.
It does not quote prices: every space is different, and the reliable number is a written quote after someone has seen it.
What drives the cost of a commercial renovation?

Mostly the building systems and the rules attached to them. Mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire protection changes, code requirements triggered by a change of use, conditions hidden in older buildings, the schedule you need, finish and equipment choices, and changes made after work starts usually explain the difference between two similar-looking projects.

blocks.x: Why do older commercial buildings cost more to renovate?

Because more is unknown until walls and ceilings open, and some of what is found must be dealt with before work can continue. Older buildings may contain asbestos, outdated wiring or past alterations that were never documented, and a change of use can bring added code requirements. Each discovery adds investigation, design and trade time.

Asbestos has its own rules. Manitoba's workplace safety regulation requires employers and owners to have asbestos-containing material inventoried by a person competent in identifying it, and treats material likely to contain asbestos as asbestos-containing until a qualified person finds otherwise. The employer or owner must notify Workplace Safety and Health 5 to 10 days before work that may release it.
Budget for testing, and for abatement if needed, before demolition starts.
How do permits and approvals affect the budget?

In three ways: fees, professional services and time. The City charges permit fees, complex work needs drawings sealed by an architect or engineer, and each review or inspection stage adds time when you may be paying rent without trading. Food premises, liquor licences and X-ray rooms each add further approvals and design requirements.

The City's commercial permit form is a useful reality check: its declared construction value includes design fees, project management fees, every sub-trade, building equipment, finishes, millwork and fixed cabinetry. See our guides to [restaurant renovation permits](/blog/restaurant-renovation-permits-winnipeg) and [clinic renovation permits](/blog/clinic-renovation-permits-winnipeg).
What drives the cost of an office, restaurant or retail renovation in Winnipeg?

Each type of space has its own expensive parts. In an office it is usually the walls, exits and building services; in a restaurant, the kitchen the health inspector reviews; in a store, the entrance, signs and lighting. These are cost drivers, not prices: each one is priced in the written quote after an on-site visit.
Office renovation costs

Office costs follow the walls and the services behind them. Demising walls between tenants affect fire separations, and the City's CADS form asks for your neighbouring tenants because those requirements depend on their uses. Significant work on exits, public corridors or fire separations in a Part 3 building needs drawings sealed by an architect or engineer.

Every new room also needs power, data, lighting and heating and cooling that suit it, and work in an occupied office often moves to evenings and weekends. Your team can move in only once the City issues an interim or final occupancy permit, where one is required, so rent paid before then belongs in the budget too.
For the lease side of those dates, see [office fit-up planning around your lease](/blog/office-fit-up-lease-planning-winnipeg).
Restaurant renovation costs

Most of the extra requirements sit in the kitchen. Manitoba's food premises guideline requires a public health inspector to review the plans before construction, and every new or renovated food premises to have an approved Type I or Type II hood suited to the menu.

The ventilation and fire suppression system is settled with the local permit authority and the inspector, and the health permit waits for the authority's written confirmation. In an existing restaurant with a Type II hood, the guideline warns that a change of owner or menu may mean upgrading the kitchen ventilation.

The guideline also calls for properly sized grease traps or interceptors serving the utensil washing sinks, built to the Manitoba Plumbing Code and easy to reach for cleaning, plus smooth, impervious floors coved and sealed 10 cm (4 inches) up the wall and easily cleaned, non-absorbent walls and ceilings in food preparation and dishwashing areas.
Licensed premises must also tell the LGCA when major renovations are made.
Retail renovation costs

Retail budgets go where customers look first: the storefront, entrance, signs and lighting. When an existing building is altered and the authority finds it isn't practical for every applicable entrance to comply with the barrier-free rules, Manitoba's amendment to the 2020 National Building Code says “at least one pedestrian entrance shall be barrier-free.”

Signs are their own line item: the City says to get a permit before starting any construction or alteration to any part of a sign, and new internally illuminated signs need a separate electrical sign permit. If the unit was last used for something other than retail, a change of use can add drawings and an occupancy permit.
What causes commercial renovation cost overruns?

Overruns usually start before construction: a scope priced from incomplete drawings, allowances that are too low, or a building that was not investigated. During the work, changes of mind, hidden conditions, late approvals and long-lead items push costs up. Most can be reduced with complete information up front and a written process for changes.
**Finish the design before pricing.** A quote is only as complete as the drawings and scope behind it.
**Investigate the building.** Look above ceilings and behind walls where possible, and get the asbestos inventory before demolition.
**Read the inclusions and exclusions.** Ask what each allowance covers and what happens if actual costs differ.
**Carry a contingency.** BDC advises setting aside a contingency fund and buffer time, because renovations often run over budget and past deadline.
**Agree how changes work.** Price and schedule each change in writing before the work is done.
**Order long-lead items early.** Mechanical units, custom millwork and specialty fixtures can set the schedule.
**Stay in touch weekly.** Bridgeland Builders sends a progress update every week, so issues surface while they are still small.
How can you lower costs without cutting quality?

Spend where it matters and simplify everywhere else. Keep plumbing and mechanical runs where they are, reuse walls, doors and ceilings in good condition, choose standard commercial materials for back-of-house areas, and phase the work if closing is the bigger cost. Value engineering looks for cheaper ways to meet the same performance, not lower standards.

Energy upgrades can lower operating costs, and some qualify for incentives: Efficiency Manitoba's Business Lighting Program says not to buy materials or start until your application is approved, so apply before ordering fixtures.

After-hours work is a trade-off too. Within 150 metres of a home, the City limits loud construction to 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends and holidays, so late shifts suit quieter tasks.
How do you get a reliable number?

From a written quote based on the actual space. Commercial work isn't priced online: every commercial project with Bridgeland Builders starts with a free on-site visit and a free written quote that sets out the scope, inclusions and exclusions. Taxes are shown on your written quote.
